digest.intro: Hidden armies, crumbling orthodoxies, and one unreasonable man in balsa wood.

items.title: 2.8 Million Military Records Stolen in Pentagon Breach — Second Federal Hack in a Month
items.blurb: The Defense Manpower Data Center was compromised starting last October; the stolen records include occupational specialties — which fields like intelligence identify as exactly the signal you'd want to map high-value targets. A month earlier, ShinyHunters claimed FBI employee records including job titles tied to China and Russia investigations. Two breaches, same window, same adversarial value.

items.title: October 18 Deadline: 100% Tariffs on Russian Oil Buyers — India and China in the Crosshairs
items.blurb: The Lindsey Graham Act imposes a statutory deadline this month forcing the US to either sanction the world's largest oil importers or visibly abandon the deterrence logic behind the law. Iran ceasefire talks stalling simultaneously in Doha means two live pressure points are converging on the same two-week window.

sections.heading: Machines and what they actually do

items.title: Ten Years After AlphaGo, Its Architect Says LLMs Still Can't Reason
items.blurb: The author helped build AlphaGo and makes a structural argument: Move 37 wasn't intuition, it was reasoning — a system that could evaluate position, simulate outcomes, and update beliefs. LLMs, he argues, have the pattern-recognition layer but not the machinery that made that move possible. Coming from someone inside the room in Seoul, this lands differently than the usual hot take.

items.title: AI Beat the World's Best Stratego Player — The Trick Was Modeling His Hidden State
items.blurb: Ataraxos beat Pim Niemeijer 15-1 with four draws, trained on just 16 GPUs. The key insight: a second neural network dedicated entirely to modeling what the opponent's hidden pieces probably are — second-order belief tracking made explicit and architectural. Where poker bots only hide 2 cards, Stratego hides 40 pieces across a game that unfolds over dozens of moves; the solution had to be structural, not brute-force.

items.title: Joe Macken Built a 50×27-Foot Model of New York Over 21 Years
items.blurb: Balsa wood and cardboard, one person, two decades — Simon Willison saw it in person at the Museum of the City of New York and says it exceeded already high expectations. The exhibition closes October 12th. If you're in New York this is the thing to see before it's gone.

items.title: Vibration Adhesion: This Mechanism Is Stranger Than Bernoulli
items.blurb: Steve Mould demonstrates a device that turns any surface into a temporary suction cup through vibration — and the mechanism turns out not to be what the obvious explanation (Bernoulli effect) would predict. Mould is one of the few science communicators who goes after the actual physics rather than the satisfying-but-wrong version.

items.title: How a Few Hundred Spaniards Toppled Two Empires of Millions
items.blurb: Military historian Si Sheppard walks through the Aztec and Inca conquests as systems problems: legitimacy cascades, network effects, and the fact that 99% of Cortés's and Pizarro's forces were drawn from the very peoples being conquered. The most clarifying frame in the episode is that this wasn't a military story — it was an information and alliance story, where the Conquistadors functioned less like an army and more like a catalyst for internal collapse. Dwarkesh notes, without overplaying it, that this is also the closest historical analogue to an 'alien force whose motives the defenders barely understand' taking over a larger established order.

facts.fact: The Pentagon breach that stole 2.8 million military personnel records began last October and went undetected for months — the stolen 'occupational specialty' field is considered especially valuable to foreign intelligence for identifying high-value targets.
Ataraxos, the AI that beat the world's best Stratego player 15-1, was trained on just 16 GPUs for a few thousand dollars — a fraction of DeepMind's budget on a problem DeepMind couldn't crack.

A diabetes study presented at EASD 2026 found that people with type 1 and type 2 diabetes sometimes reported better quality of life after days when their glucose fluctuated more — provided levels stayed within safe limits — suggesting the effort to eliminate every fluctuation carries its own hidden cost.

Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca Empire of roughly 10 million people with a force in which native allies constituted approximately 99% of his troops — the conquest was structurally an internal collapse, not an external invasion.

Joe Macken's model of New York City — 50 by 27 feet, built from balsa wood and cardboard over 21 years by one person — is currently on display at the Museum of the City of New York and closes October 12th.

art_picks.title: Leviathan
art_picks.creator: Lucien Castaing-Taylor & Véréna Paravel (Sensory Ethnography Lab, 2012)
art_picks.why: Shot entirely on GoPros lashed to nets, decks, and fish — it dissolves the boundary between camera and environment until you can't tell where the ocean ends and the hull begins. No narration, no explanation, pure system-as-sensation: a film that turns industrial labor into something almost geological.

art_picks.title: The Atlas Group Archive
art_picks.creator: Walid Raad
art_picks.why: A meticulous fake archive documenting the Lebanese civil wars — fabricated documents, invented historians, plausible footnotes. Raad built an entire epistemology of trauma out of institutional aesthetics, turning the grammar of evidence into a meditation on how collective memory hardens into fact. Category-blurring at its most elegant: art that functions as mythology, history, and con simultaneously.

art_picks.title: Replica
art_picks.creator: Oneohtrix Point Never
art_picks.why: Daniel Lopatin built this entirely from late-night TV commercial samples, then ran them through such extreme processing that the familiar becomes alien — consumer jingles as archaeological material, nostalgia as texture rather than sentiment. A record about how pop culture colonizes memory, made from pop culture's corpse.

events.name: Thomas Ruff: jpegs ny
events.why: Ruff sourced low-res internet images of 9/11, maxed their JPEG compression, added color, and blew them to the scale of 19th-century history painting — the pixel grid becomes brushstroke, and the most over-documented event in living memory becomes genuinely hard to look at again; closes next Friday.

events.name: Tone (group exhibition)
events.venue: The Studio Museum in Harlem, 144 West 125th Street
events.why: Nineteen artists — Roy DeCarava, Kerry James Marshall, Lorna Simpson among them — organized around a single formal question: what does value (black to white and everything between) carry as expressive language? A show built on a system, not a theme.

events.name: Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous
events.venue: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1000 Fifth Avenue
events.why: The Met hangs Krasner and Pollock canvas-to-canvas across the years they shared a house in Springs — a rare curatorial move that reframes both bodies of work as a live conversation rather than separate careers; opens Saturday.

events.name: CLEA RSKY: Stephen Dean
events.venue: CLEA RSKY, 925 Bergen Street, Crown Heights, Brooklyn
events.why: Dean's work lives at the intersection of color, duration, and ritual — saturated, time-based pieces that use ceremony and crowd behavior as raw material; a niche Crown Heights space makes this a genuine find over the Chelsea circuit.
